TidyVerse CREATE: Exploring College Major Earnings with dplyr, ggplot2, and tidyr

Introduction

This vignette demonstrates core capabilities of three TidyVerse packages: dplyr, ggplot2, and tidyr, using the college_recent_grads dataset from the fivethirtyeight package.

Note: to install fivethirtyeight in the console: install.packages("fivethirtyeight")

Load Libraries and Data

library(tidyverse)
library(fivethirtyeight)

data("college_recent_grads")
glimpse(college_recent_grads)

Part 1: dplyr – Selecting, Filtering, and Summarizing

select() – Pick the columns you need

select() lets you keep only the columns relevant to your analysis, which makes data frames easier to read and work with.

major_earnings <- college_recent_grads |>
  select(major, major_category, total, median, p25th, p75th, unemployment_rate)

head(major_earnings)
## # A tibble: 6 × 7
##   major               major_category total median p25th  p75th unemployment_rate
##   <chr>               <chr>          <int>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>             <dbl>
## 1 Petroleum Engineer… Engineering     2339 110000 95000 125000            0.0184
## 2 Mining And Mineral… Engineering      756  75000 55000  90000            0.117 
## 3 Metallurgical Engi… Engineering      856  73000 50000 105000            0.0241
## 4 Naval Architecture… Engineering     1258  70000 43000  80000            0.0501
## 5 Chemical Engineeri… Engineering    32260  65000 50000  75000            0.0611
## 6 Nuclear Engineering Engineering     2573  65000 50000 102000            0.177

filter() – Subset rows by condition

filter() keeps only the rows that satisfy a logical condition. Here we pull out majors where the median salary exceeds $50,000.

high_earning <- major_earnings |>
  filter(median > 50000)

high_earning |>
  select(major, major_category, median) |>
  arrange(desc(median))
## # A tibble: 25 × 3
##    major                                     major_category    median
##    <chr>                                     <chr>              <dbl>

##  3 Metallurgical Engineering                 Engineering        73000

mutate() – Create new columns

mutate() adds new columns that are functions of existing ones. We can compute an interquartile range (IQR) of earnings to measure salary spread within each major.

major_earnings <- major_earnings |>
  mutate(iqr_earnings = p75th - p25th)

major_earnings |>
  select(major, median, iqr_earnings) |>
  arrange(desc(iqr_earnings)) |>
  head(10)
## # A tibble: 10 × 3
##    major                                               median iqr_earnings

group_by() + summarize() – Aggregate by category

group_by() splits the data by a categorical variable, and summarize() computes summary statistics for each group. This is one of the most powerful patterns in dplyr.

category_summary <- major_earnings |>
  group_by(major_category) |>
  summarize(
    n_majors       = n(),
    median_salary  = median(median, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_unemp     = mean(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_salary))

arrange() – Sort your results

We already used arrange() above, but it deserves its own callout. Sorting by a computed summary makes it easy to spot the top and bottom categories at a glance.

Agriculture and Natural Resources has both a respectable median salary and the lowest average unemployment rate among these categories.

Part 2: ggplot2 – Visualizing the Data

Bar chart – Median salary by major category

geom_col() draws bars whose heights correspond to values in the data (as opposed to geom_bar(), which counts rows). coord_flip() makes long category labels readable.

ggplot(category_summary, aes(x = reorder(major_category, median_salary),
                              y = median_salary)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Salary by Major Category",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median Salary ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Scatter plot – Salary vs. unemployment rate

Each point is one major. geom_smooth() overlays a LOESS trend line so we can see whether higher-paying majors tend to have lower unemployment.

ggplot(major_earnings, aes(x = unemployment_rate, y = median)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = major_category), alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Salary vs. Unemployment Rate by Major",
    x = "Unemployment Rate",
    y = "Median Salary ($)",
    color = "Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 7))

Box plot – Salary distributions within categories

Box plots reveal the spread and outliers within each category, not just the center.

ggplot(major_earnings, aes(x = reorder(major_category, median, FUN = stats::median),
                            y = median)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue", outlier.color = "red") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Median Salaries Within Each Major Category",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median Salary ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Part 3: tidyr – Reshaping Data

pivot_longer() – Wide to long format

Many ggplot geometries work best with “long” data, where each row is a single observation. The salary percentile columns (p25th, median, p75th) are currently spread across three columns. pivot_longer() stacks them into one column so we can map the percentile label to color or facet.

top5 <- major_earnings |>
  arrange(desc(median)) |>
  head(5)

top5_long <- top5 |>
  select(major, p25th, median, p75th) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(p25th, median, p75th),
    names_to  = "percentile",
    values_to = "salary"
  )

top5_long
## # A tibble: 15 × 3
##    major                                     percentile salary
##    <chr>                                     <chr>       <dbl>
##  1 Petroleum Engineering                     p25th       95000
##  2 Petroleum Engineering                     median     110000
##  3 Petroleum Engineering                     p75th      125000
##  4 Mining And Mineral Engineering            p25th       55000
##  5 Mining And Mineral Engineering            median      75000
##  6 Mining And Mineral Engineering            p75th       90000
##  7 Metallurgical Engineering                 p25th       50000
##  8 Metallurgical Engineering                 median      73000
##  9 Metallurgical Engineering                 p75th      105000
## 10 Naval Architecture And Marine Engineering p25th       43000
## 11 Naval Architecture And Marine Engineering median      70000
## 12 Naval Architecture And Marine Engineering p75th       80000
## 13 Chemical Engineering                      p25th       50000
## 14 Chemical Engineering                      median      65000
## 15 Chemical Engineering                      p75th       75000

Visualizing the reshaped data

Now that we have long-format data, a grouped bar chart comparing the three percentiles for each major is straightforward.

top5_long <- top5_long |>
  mutate(percentile = factor(percentile,
                             levels = c("p25th", "median", "p75th"),
                             labels = c("25th Pctile", "Median", "75th Pctile")))

ggplot(top5_long, aes(x = reorder(major, salary), y = salary, fill = percentile)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  labs(
    title = "Salary Percentiles for Top 5 Earning Majors",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Salary ($)",
    fill = "Percentile"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

pivot_wider() – Long back to wide

pivot_wider() is the inverse operation. If a downstream model or table expects one column per percentile, you can spread the data back out.

top5_wide <- top5_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = percentile,
    values_from = salary
  )

top5_wide
## # A tibble: 5 × 4
##   major                                     `25th Pctile` Median `75th Pctile`
##   <chr>                                             <dbl>  <dbl>         <dbl>
## 1 Petroleum Engineering                             95000 110000        125000
## 2 Mining And Mineral Engineering                    55000  75000         90000
## 3 Metallurgical Engineering                         50000  73000        105000
## 4 Naval Architecture And Marine Engineering         43000  70000         80000
## 5 Chemical Engineering                              50000  65000         75000

Conclusion

This vignette walked through the core verbs of three TidyVerse packages:

  • dplyr: select(), filter(), mutate(), group_by(), summarize(), arrange()
  • ggplot2: geom_col(), geom_point(), geom_smooth(), geom_boxplot()
  • tidyr: pivot_longer(), pivot_wider()

Together these tools cover a typical analysis workflow: subset and transform the data, compute summaries, reshape for plotting, and visualize the results.
